what_it_does: Running large AI language models with heavily compressed (low-bit) weights requires multiplying small integers against full-precision numbers — an operation that today's GPU math units do not support natively, forcing expensive workarounds. LUT Tensor Core replaces these multiplications with precomputed lookup tables, and solves the two problems that previously made that approach impractical: the tables were too expensive to build and too large to store efficiently.
method_in_detail:
The idea. When AI model weights are compressed to 1, 2, or 4 bits, every weight can only take a handful of distinct values. Instead of multiplying a weight by an activation value on the fly, you can precompute all possible products for a small group of activations and put them in a lookup table. Inference then just reads the right answer from the table using the weight bits as an index. The catch is that building that table and broadcasting it to every processing element in a GPU's math array was previously more expensive than just doing the multiplication.

How it works. On the software side, LUT Tensor Core uses a graph transformation: the table-building step is split into its own independent kernel, computed once and shared across all math units instead of being recomputed thousands of times. That kernel is then fused with the preceding activation-processing step, so its memory cost nearly vanishes. Separately, weights are reinterpreted from {0,1} to {-1,+1}: this symmetry means the lookup table has an odd-function structure, so only half the entries are needed — the other half are just negations. On the hardware side, the math unit (the Tensor Core — a grid of multiplier-accumulator circuits inside the GPU) is redesigned to use multiplexers (electronic switches) instead of multipliers, since table lookup is just selecting a precomputed value. A bit-serial approach — processing one bit of the weight at a time across multiple clock cycles — lets a single hardware design handle weights of any bit-width without separate circuits for each case.

The key design choice. The tile shape of the math array is made 'elongated': small M dimension (2), large N dimension (64), and fixed K=4. This shape maximizes the number of output elements that can share a single lookup table, amortizing the table's cost across 64 simultaneous outputs.

The result. Compared to a conventional GPU math unit, the LUT Tensor Core uses only 16% of the chip area while matching or exceeding performance on the mixed-precision multiply. End-to-end LLM inference is 2x–8x faster depending on model and batch size. Against the best prior LUT-based hardware design, LUT Tensor Core achieves 1.44x better compute density and energy efficiency.
